article_title: Twig Science
citation: Twig Science — Evidence Rating: Promising. (2025). Imagine Learning program evidence summary. https://www.imaginelearning.com
title: 5E instructional model structure (Engage, Explore, Explain, Elaborate, Evaluate) as the organizing lesson pattern
description: Twig Science organizes instruction around the 5E model, which the summary spells out as "Engage, Explore, Explain, Elaborate, Evaluate." Within this structure the curriculum places student inquiry at the center, embeds science and engineering practices, and sequences multimedia-rich investigations and collaborative tasks across the phases. Built-in literacy supports are integrated rather than treated separately.
requirements: Implementation in each classroom by one instructional teacher, with optional curriculum training varying by grade level.
constraints: Alignment is stated for the Next Generation Science Standards; no other standards alignment is claimed.
target_learning_goals: Inquiry-based science understanding
Science and engineering practices
examples: The curriculum's investigations and collaborative tasks are delivered through the 5E phases across Grades K–8.
key_sources: Twig Science — Evidence Rating: Promising. (2025). Imagine Learning program evidence summary. https://evidenceforessa.org/program/twig-science/

article_title: 12 Heuristics for Learning Analytics in Simulation-Based Professional Learning
citation: Susan Harrington and Charlott Sellberg. (2026). 12 Heuristics for Learning Analytics in Simulation-Based Professional Learning. Journal of Learning Analytics, 13(1), 130-142. https://doi.org/10.18608/jla.2026.9141
title: Twelve LXD heuristics for evaluating learning analytics in simulation-based professional learning
description: The article's core artifact is a set of twelve heuristics organized across four dimensions: technical-pedagogical (e.g., "Enable appropriate assessment of individual and group performance", "Support temporal and spatial awareness of unfolding scenarios"), socio-technical (fostering professional vision, integrating with existing tools), socio-pedagogical (role-playing, socialization into professional values, professional language), and ethical (appropriate data use, privacy, accessibility). The heuristics are intended "to be used as a type of mnemonic in prompting the evaluator to think carefully and critically about features of the LA system".
requirements: Application during early prototyping to align design decisions with intended learning goals
Evaluation should focus on how the system supports learning outcomes, not only technical usability
constraints: The heuristics do not address potential technical issues related to system functionality or usability; established heuristics such as Nielsen's should be used for those
Developed with a relatively small group of experts and only two iterations
Applied only to early-stage prototypes, not a fully functional implementation
target_learners: UX and LX designers evaluating learning analytics systems
target_learning_goals: evaluation of learning analytics dashboards supporting professional skill development in simulators
examples: Heuristic 1 advises offering instant alerts for basic tasks while saving more detailed feedback for the post-simulation debriefing to avoid interfering with learning
key_sources: Susan Harrington and Charlott Sellberg. (2026). 12 Heuristics for Learning Analytics in Simulation-Based Professional Learning. Journal of Learning Analytics, 13(1), 130-142. https://doi.org/10.18608/jla.2026.9141

article_title: What Further Research Is Needed on Restorative Justice in Schools?
citation: Hurley, N., Guckenburg, S., Persson, H., Fronius, T., & Petrosino, A. (2015). What Further Research is Needed on Restorative Justice in Schools? WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: Two overarching perspectives on what restorative justice in schools is: whole-school philosophy versus skill-based stand-alone practice
description: The article identifies two competing expert perspectives on RJ in schools. One treats RJ as "a philosophy, as a 'way of being,'" requiring a whole-school or whole-community approach to culture and climate. The other treats RJ as "fundamentally a skill-based exercise" that staff can learn through training and use as a stand-alone strategy for individual disciplinary actions, without opposing whole-system approaches. The article notes the definitional challenge stems partly from respondents' diverse backgrounds and that research is needed on critical program elements under either approach.
requirements: A working definition of RJ that school communities can embrace, which nearly all respondents identified as needed
constraints: The two perspectives are attributed to experts and practitioners with varied backgrounds and diverse experiences, not empirically tested in this brief
target_learning_goals: restoring relationships after conflict as an alternative to punitive discipline
examples: The brief contrasts schools adopting RJ as whole-community culture change with schools using it as an add-on program focused on individual disciplinary actions
key_sources: Hurley, N., Guckenburg, S., Persson, H., Fronius, T., & Petrosino, A. (2015). What Further Research is Needed on Restorative Justice in Schools? WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED559727

article_title: The Landscape of Middle School Career and Technical Education in Nebraska
citation: Torre Gibney, T., Fong, P., Lewis, J., Maduli, D., & Castellano, M. (2024). The landscape of middle school career and technical education in Nebraska. WestEd. https://WestEd.org
title: Two common national models for middle school CTE delivery: career field–specific introductory coursework and stand-alone career exploration courses
description: The report identifies, based on interviews with national CTE experts, two common middle school delivery models: "introductory CTE coursework that puts middle grade students on a pathway to high school CTE programs", whether career field–specific or rotational, and "semester- or year-long career exploration courses focused on self-awareness and career awareness". Nebraska practice reflects both: career field–specific exploratory or introductory courses across six career fields, and generalized career development and exploration courses such as Middle School Career Development. Nationally, experts report no consensus about which model middle grades should offer.
requirements: Middle school introductory CTE courses are not formally part of a sequenced program of study; local contexts use them to recruit students into future high school CTE coursework.
constraints: Across and within states, middle grade CTE and career development programming are very uneven, and there is no consensus about whether middle grades should offer introductory CTE courses or stand-alone career exploration courses.
target_learning_goals: Career awareness and exploration
Connecting academics to career and college possibilities
Self-awareness and informed education and career decision making
examples: Lincoln Public Schools requires semester-long FCS and STS courses in grades 6–7 with grade 8 electives; Elkhorn Public Schools uses six-week exploratory rotations; Omaha and Millard offer exploratory CTE as electives in a six-week rotation.
key_sources: Torre Gibney, T., Fong, P., Lewis, J., Maduli, D., & Castellano, M. (2024). The landscape of middle school career and technical education in Nebraska. WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED673552

article_title: Beyond Tool Adoption: A Practical Five-Stage Developmental Continuum for AI Literacy in Higher Education
citation: Liu, J. P., & Levy, R. (2026). Beyond Tool Adoption: A Practical Five-Stage Developmental Continuum for AI Literacy in Higher Education. North Carolina State University.
title: Two-day intensive training agenda sequenced to move learners from Stage 0 through Stage 4 transitions
description: Table 5 maps each activity of the 2-day hands-on AI/LLM training to the stage transition it facilitates: demystification of platforms moves Stage 0 to 1; hands-on API use, local model deployment, and RAG-based verification move Stage 1 to 2; tool evaluation, fine-tuning concepts, and bias detection move Stage 2 to 3; advanced fine-tuning, auto-coding agents, and building a small language model from scratch move Stage 3 to 4. The article reports this as "a practical pathway from Stage 0 (Not Yet Engaged) through Stage 4 (Improvement) within an intensive 2-day format."
requirements: Well-structured sequencing of activities aligned to intended stage transitions
constraints: Evidence for resulting stage movement is observational and practice-based, not from validated pre/post measurement
target_learning_goals: moving from AI avoidance to informed use
verification of AI outputs
AI system improvement skills
examples: Day 1 activities include running LLMs locally with Ollama and RAG with tokenization, embeddings, and vector databases; Day 2 includes QLoRA/PEFT fine-tuning and building a GPT-2/3-like model from scratch
key_sources: Liu, J. P., & Levy, R. (2026). Beyond Tool Adoption: A Practical Five-Stage Developmental Continuum for AI Literacy in Higher Education. North Carolina State University. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.00038

article_title: AI in the Wild: A Large Scale Analysis of Authentic Interactions of College Students with Generative AI
citation: Taelin Karidi, Ofra Amir, and Ido Roll. (2026). AI in the Wild: A Large Scale Analysis of Authentic Interactions of College Students with Generative AI. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.29442
title: Two-dimensional annotation framework: cognitive intent (Bloom level) and interaction context
description: The article introduces a two-dimensional annotation framework for characterizing student–AI interaction units. Dimension 1 captures the "cognitive intentunderlying each student turn", operationalized with Bloom's revised taxonomy (remember, understand, apply, analyze, evaluate, create). Dimension 2 captures the "interaction context, specifying what the student is directing the AI to engage with": own_work, task_domain, ai_output, or administrative. The framework was informed by established educational taxonomies and developed through iterative inspection of authentic interactions.
requirements: Annotations are assigned at the interaction unit level based on the inferred intent expressed in the student's message, with the AI response used only as contextual information when the request is underspecified.
constraints: Bloom's taxonomy "remains agnostic to the object of that request", which motivates the second dimension; the framework was applied via an LLM-based procedure without human-agreement evaluation in this study.
target_learners: undergraduate students using generative AI in coursework
target_learning_goals: characterizing how students engage generative AI during authentic academic work
examples: Applied with gpt-5-mini to annotate 15,887 interaction turns from 821 students across six courses, revealing distinct course-level interaction profiles.
key_sources: Taelin Karidi, Ofra Amir, and Ido Roll. (2026). AI in the Wild: A Large Scale Analysis of Authentic Interactions of College Students with Generative AI. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.29442

article_title: A Longitudinal Analysis of Public Discourse on AI Ethics in Education Using Twitter Data
citation: Bagale, A.; Mehjabin, N.; Ünlü, A.; Johri, A. (2025). A Longitudinal Analysis of Public Discourse on AI Ethics in Education Using Twitter Data.
title: Five-year Twitter corpus (14,201 tweets) with SetFit sentiment classifier and BERTopic modelling pipeline
description: A corpus of 14,201 English-language tweets from U.S.-based users (January 2019–November 2024) collected via twarc2 and Twitter's Academic Research API with combined AI/education/ethics search terms. Sentiment was classified with a SetFit classifier (validation accuracy 89%, macro F1 0.88) and themes extracted with BERTopic, reduced to 16 topics. Data and code are available from the authors upon request.
requirements: Access to Twitter's Academic Research API and adherence to its Terms of Service for collecting the tweet corpus
constraints: Restricted to Twitter/X, English-language, U.S.-based users; the platform's engagement-optimizing algorithm may overrepresent emotionally charged posts
target_learners: researchers studying public discourse on educational technology
target_learning_goals: understanding public perceptions of AI ethics in education
examples: The corpus underpins the monthly sentiment timeline and the 16-topic BERTopic model reported in the study's results.
key_sources: Bagale, A.; Mehjabin, N.; Ünlü, A.; Johri, A. (2025). A Longitudinal Analysis of Public Discourse on AI Ethics in Education Using Twitter Data. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.12295

article_title: Educational Innovation through Automated Essay Scoring: A Multidimensional Framework for Evaluating Critical Thinking in High School Physics Essays
citation: Firdausi, H.; Wasis; Sholikah, R. W.; Lemantara, J.; Rosyadi, F. D.; Ginardi, R. V. H.; Pradityo, M. H. A.; Hakim, A. R. (2026). Educational Innovation through Automated Essay Scoring: A Multidimensional Framework for Evaluating Critical Thinking in High School Physics Essays. International Journal of Intelligent Engineering and Systems, Vol.19, No.8. https://doi.org/10.22266/ijies2026.0831.09
title: Two-stage data preparation pipeline: rule-based synthetic generation plus LLM paraphrase augmentation without data leakage
description: The pipeline first generates synthetic score-level-1 samples in the training partition only, using "template-based generation (40%), quality degradation (35%), and a combined approach (25%)", including truncation to 20–40% of original length and removal of domain-critical keywords. Second, paraphrase-based augmentation via the Gemini API balances minority classes at scores 2–4 to a uniform 25% per level. Splitting was done once at the student level so each student's responses appear in a single partition, "thereby preventing cross -dimensional data leakage," and the test set stayed locked and unmodified.
requirements: Augmentation and generation confined strictly to the training partition; fixed random seed; target counts set to the majority class size per dimension
constraints: Alternative techniques (back-translation, synonym substitution, EDA) were excluded after preliminary experiments showed lower output quality and inconsistent meaning preservation in the Indonesian physics essay domain; in Overview, augmentation marginally decreased QWK
target_learners: Indonesian high school physics students whose essays form the scored dataset
target_learning_goals: Reliable ordinal automated scoring of critical thinking dimensions despite severe class imbalance
examples: After augmentation, training-set sizes ranged from 148 (Reason) to 212 (Inference) samples per dimension, with the test set fixed at 23 samples throughout

article_title: Teaching Students to Question the Machine: An AI Literacy Intervention Improves Students' Regulation of LLM Use in a Science Task
citation: Olivier Clerc, Rania Abdelghani, Chloé Desvaux, Eliott Poisson, Pierre-Yves Oudeyer, Hélène Sauzéon. (2026). Teaching Students to Question the Machine: Short-Term Effects of an AI Literacy Workshop on Middle-School Students’ Regulation of LLM Interaction. ALIT4ALL 2026: 2nd International Workshop on AI Literacy Education For All. https://osf.io/fyu7c/overview
title: Two-hour classroom AI literacy workshop combining LLM concepts with agency-preserving regulation practice
description: A two-hour, classroom-feasible workshop with a conceptual component on "how LLMs generate text, why they can produce incomplete or incorrect answers" and a practical component that "did not rehearse the later experimental science tasks". Students discussed common LLM output problems, then in small groups predicted whether prompts would elicit satisfactory responses, queried an LLM, evaluated answers, and revised prompts as needed. The slide deck and facilitation script are released in an OSF repository.
requirements: A classroom setting with LLM chatbot access for the practical prompting activities
constraints: The workshop did not rehearse the experimental science tasks, so effects tested transfer of a general regulatory stance
Materials are currently available in French
target_learning_goals: applied regulation of LLM interaction: prompting, response evaluation, and follow-up questioning during science problem solving
examples: Students received a task goal and an initial prompt, predicted whether the prompt was likely to elicit a satisfactory response, queried the LLM, evaluated the answer, and revised the prompt or continued the interaction when needed

article_title: Data Comics for Education: Evaluating Effectiveness, Benefits, and the Ethics of AI-Assisted Creation
citation: Zirui Shan, Vanessa Echeverria, Yuheng Li, Yi-Shan Tsai, and Roberto Martinez-Maldonado. (2026). Data Comics for Education: Evaluating Effectiveness, Benefits, and the Ethics of AI-Assisted Creation. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02361
title: Two-stage data comic creation pattern separating human-led narrative design from human–AI co-creation of visual elements
description: The article describes a two-stage production process for building data comics with GenAI assistance. In Stage 1, a researcher extracts key insights and classifies them into Bach et al.'s content relation categories, mapping them onto panel layouts, with reviewers validating choices. In Stage 2, image elements are generated with DALL-E 3 via ChatGPT-4, integrated into pre-defined panel layouts, and assembled with storytelling elements in Canva. The authors state the process separated "human-led narrative design from the human–AI co-creation of visual elements".
requirements: Researcher expertise in data science, visual analytics, and visualisation or dashboard design to extract insights and review outputs
Established data comic design patterns (Bach et al.) to structure content relation and layout decisions
GenAI text-to-image tooling (DALL-E 3 via ChatGPT-4) and an assembly tool (Canva)
constraints: Comics were created by researchers, not students or teachers, so the process is described for expert-led production
The article does not report effects of the process itself, only of the resulting comics
target_learning_goals: interpreting and reasoning with visual data
comprehending data-driven insights
examples: Four data comics on climate change data were produced this way and compared against four matched conventional visualisations in a within-subjects study with 60 students
key_sources: Zirui Shan, Vanessa Echeverria, Yuheng Li, Yi-Shan Tsai, and Roberto Martinez-Maldonado. (2026). Data Comics for Education: Evaluating Effectiveness, Benefits, and the Ethics of AI-Assisted Creation. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02361

article_title: DebugTracker: Lightweight Process Evidence for Classroom Debugging
citation: Jiatong Liu, Xue Yao, Zehua Zhang, and Yongqiang Tian. (2026). DebugTracker: Lightweight Process Evidence for Classroom Debugging. Companion Proceedings of the 2026 ACM SIGPLAN International Conference on Systems, Programming, Languages, and Applications: Software for Humanity (SPLASH Companion '26). https://doi.org/10.1145/3837729.3840500
title: Separating coached practice traces from uncoached assessment traces in process evidence capture
description: DebugTracker structures each recording session into one of two mutually exclusive modes. "Evaluation Mode is uncoached: it disables process prompts, solution hints, and after-session feedback, and marks its reports as assessment traces", while Training Mode provides process prompts and optional AI feedback. This explicit mode boundary keeps coached practice traces separate from assessment evidence so instructors can trust what an assessment trace contains.
requirements: Students must select a mode at session start; the tooling must disable coaching features in assessment mode and label reports accordingly
constraints: The two modes differ only in coaching; the article states the coaching "never reveals the fix or patches the code for the student"
target_learners: Students completing debugging exercises in programming courses
target_learning_goals: Debugging process competence that can be assessed without coaching contamination
examples: In the demonstration the presenter selects the Evaluation Mode path, runs python -m unittest, and the exported report is labeled a Student Summary (Evaluation)
key_sources: Jiatong Liu, Xue Yao, Zehua Zhang, and Yongqiang Tian. (2026). DebugTracker: Lightweight Process Evidence for Classroom Debugging. Companion Proceedings of the 2026 ACM SIGPLAN International Conference on Systems, Programming, Languages, and Applications: Software for Humanity (SPLASH Companion '26). https://doi.org/10.1145/3837729.3840500

article_title: Embodied Inquiry with AI as Facilitator: An Exploratory Case Study
citation: Eugenio Tufino, Paola Damiani. (2026). Embodied inquiry with AI as facilitator: an exploratory case study. https://udlguidelines.cast.org
title: Design AI facilitation in two phases: embodied model-building stays human first, and the AI enters only afterward on the epistemic layer
description: The article proposes a division of labour in which students build the physics model with their own hands, instruments and shared meaning before any AI enters, and a language-based facilitator then facilitates application of the model to a new phenomenon. In the study's words, the embodied inquiry came first and stayed human, and the facilitator entered later on the epistemic layer, where its channel suffices, making the AI a complement to embodied inquiry rather than a substitute for it.
requirements: The boundary of the facilitator must be planned from the start and made visible to the students themselves
constraints: Fragility: under student pressure the facilitator crossed from scaffolding reasoning to inventing data, so fidelity must be checked rather than assumed
target_learners: university students in laboratory physics courses
target_learning_goals: applying and extending a student-built physics model to a new phenomenon while preserving embodied experience
examples: Students built the buoyancy model without AI in phase one; in phase two a custom Gem named “Physics ISLE Lab process” facilitated applying it to floating drink cans
key_sources: Eugenio Tufino, Paola Damiani. (2026). Embodied inquiry with AI as facilitator: an exploratory case study. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21349

article_title: Bridging Artificial Intelligence and Power Systems Education Using a Hands-On Executable Framework
citation: Junjie Yin, Buxin She, Xinyu Feng, Fangxing (Fran) Li. (2026). Bridging Artificial Intelligence and Power Systems Education Using a Hands-On Executable Framework. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02599
title: Two-map pairing framework: coupling an AI knowledge map to a power-system knowledge map
description: The framework organizes teaching around two complementary knowledge maps: an AI map ordered by problem type (nonlinear regression, structured feature extraction, constrained decision making, sequential decision making, physics-constrained learning) and a power-system map ordered by task function (forecasting, power-flow analysis, dispatch, storage control, dynamics). "The core idea of the framework is topairentries across the two maps rather than teach them in isolation." Each module keeps the same generic AI workflow but anchors it in a recognizable power-system problem, directly addressing the survey finding that image-classification exemplars feel disconnected from power engineering.
requirements: Every module must deliberately couple a core AI concept to a representative power-system task so learners see why the method matters
constraints: Modules are arranged in three tiers of increasing conceptual and engineering complexity, from foundational supervised learning to research-edge methods
target_learners: beginners, students, practitioners, and interdisciplinary learners in power and energy systems
target_learning_goals: core AI concepts (regression, convolution, learned constraints, DRL, physics-informed learning) as applied to power-system tasks
examples: Function approximation is paired with load-curve prediction; convolution with a power-flow surrogate; a learned constraint with security-constrained decision making; DRL with battery storage control; physics-informed training with the swing equation.
key_sources: Junjie Yin, Buxin She, Xinyu Feng, Fangxing (Fran) Li. (2026). Bridging Artificial Intelligence and Power Systems Education Using a Hands-On Executable Framework. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02599

article_title: Distilling Black-Box Machine Learning into a Small, Self-Explaining Language Model for Learning Analytics
citation: Chenguang Pan, Airui Meng, and Youmi Suk. (2026). Distilling Black-Box Machine Learning into a Small, Self-Explaining Language Model for Learning Analytics. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.21165
title: Two-stage mentor–mentee distillation pipeline for self-explaining predictive LLMs
description: The pipeline first fits a flexible ML estimator and interprets it with ALE-fANOVA decomposition, then fine-tunes a small open-weight LLM on mentor traces with LoRA. The authors state the design is "estimator-agnostic and paired with a faithfulness-first evaluation framework that audits every narration against the attribution it claims to describe." Unlike prior designs in which the LLM merely restates an explanation another system provides, this mentee produces the estimate, decisions, and explanation itself. Deployment requires only a small model interacting in natural language.
requirements: An upstream fitted estimator that returns an individual-level estimate and a decomposition-based interpretation tool (ALE-fANOVA)
constraints: The pipeline treats the upstream estimator's output as a black box, so errors in the estimator propagate to the distilled model
Requires acceptance-gated validation of mentor traces before training
target_learners: Students, parents, counselors, and classroom-level educational stakeholders
target_learning_goals: Interpreting individual-level predictions and treatment-effect estimates to support educational decision-making
examples: Instantiated on an X-learner causal estimator with the HSLS:09 dataset, producing a fine-tuned Gemma E2B that maps a student's covariate profile to an effect estimate, explanation, and recommended action
key_sources: Chenguang Pan, Airui Meng, and Youmi Suk. (2026). Distilling Black-Box Machine Learning into a Small, Self-Explaining Language Model for Learning Analytics. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.21165

article_title: Not All Students Engage Alike: Multi-Institution Patterns in GenAI Tutor Use
citation: Youjie Chen, Xixi Shi, Xinyu Liu, Shuaiguo Wang, Tracy Xiao Liu, Dragan Gašević. (2026). Not All Students Engage Alike: Multi-Institution Patterns in GenAI Tutor Use. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.00447
title: Two-stage learning analytics framework for GenAI Tutor engagement: session-level engagement types plus student-level transition patterns
description: The article proposes a learning analytics framework that first identifies engagement types at the conversation session level through clustering on behavioral, cognitive, and temporal features, then aggregates them into student-level engagement patterns via process mining. The authors state they "propose a learning analytics framework that identifies conversation session-level engagement types and integrates with student-level engagement patterns, which can be applied to other human-AI interaction data." It builds on prior process-mining work that segments logs into sessions and aggregates tactics into strategies.
requirements: Requires student-GenAI interaction logs with prompts, responses, and timestamps, plus engineered behavioral, cognitive, and temporal features
constraints: Emotional engagement was not characterized because the authors lacked approaches to reliably infer emotions from their data logs
target_learning_goals: understanding and improving student engagement with GenAI tutoring tools
examples: Applied to 113,255 conversation sessions from 11,406 students across 200 classes at ten institutions, segmented with a 15-minute threshold plus LLM topic segmentation achieving an F1-score of 0.9

article_title: What Don't You Understand? Using Large Language Models to Identify and Characterize Student Misconceptions About Challenging Topics
citation: Parker, M. J., & Zavala-Cerna, M. G. (2025). What Don't You Understand? Using Large Language Models to Identify and Characterize Student Misconceptions About Challenging Topics. https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.09875
title: Two-stage LLM misconception identification pipeline (GPT-4 misconception analysis plus Gemini topic synopses)
description: A pipeline combining quantitative quiz analysis with two LLM stages: GPT-4 (gpt-4o-2024-08-06, temperature 0.3) generates hypothesized misconceptions from structured question representations, most common incorrect answers, and Whisper-transcribed lecture transcripts; Gemini 2.0 Flash (temperature 0) creates topic synopses from titles and transcripts for instructors. The total LLM cost was minimal, "with the misconceptions work requiring only approximately one dollar and the topic synopsis work requiring one cent". The pipeline ran on an ordinary laptop via cloud APIs.

Lecture video transcripts (generated via Whisper large-v2)
Python coding skills for API-based batch processing
constraints: Drag-and-drop questions were excluded from misconception analysis due to difficulty of automatic characterization
Chat-based LLM interfaces lack reproducibility and reliable structured output compared to API access
target_learners: medical students in online biomedical science courses
target_learning_goals: characterizing student misconceptions on challenging topics
examples: Processed 20-36 problems per course across five course types (140 total) at a total cost of approximately $1.07 for all LLM calls

article_title: Four Types of LLM Reliance and Their Predictors Among Undergraduate Writers: A Mixed-Methods Study at a Minority-Serving R1 University
citation: Shahin Hossain. (2026). Four Types of LLM Reliance and Their Predictors Among Undergraduate Writers: A Mixed-Methods Study at a Minority-Serving R1 University. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.28749
title: Two-Tier Predictive Architecture of LLM Reliance: AI Literacy determines type direction, Expectancy-Value beliefs determine intensity, structured by Biggs' 3P Model
description: The article integrates three frameworks into a two-tier predictive architecture for LLM reliance. At the predictive level, the AI Literacy Framework accounts for the type of reliance students adopt, while Expectancy-Value Theory explains the intensity of reliance; at the structural level, Biggs' Presage-Process-Product Model supplies the architecture connecting presage factors, reliance behavior, and writing outcomes. The article states these frameworks form "separate yet interlocking explanatory systems," and that "AI literacy and EVT beliefs function as distinct, non-redundant predictors." The architecture underpins the study's four-type taxonomy and its claim that interventions targeting one dimension will not affect the other.
requirements: Measurement of both AI literacy (knowledge, evaluation, ethics) and Expectancy-Value beliefs as separate predictor systems
Classification of reliance type via subscale means against a defined endorsement threshold
constraints: The article notes non-significant moderation findings should be interpreted as inconclusive because the achieved sample was slightly below the moderation power target
target_learning_goals: Academic writing with generative AI
AI literacy and ethical engagement with LLMs
key_sources: Shahin Hossain. (2026). Four Types of LLM Reliance and Their Predictors Among Undergraduate Writers: A Mixed-Methods Study at a Minority-Serving R1 University. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.28749

article_title: From Evaluated Models to Evaluation Aids: A Multi-Evidence Study of LLM-Based Difficulty Calibration for Programming Examinations
citation: Hongfei Yan, Jiangkai Xiong, Yiqing Li, and Chong Chen. (2026). From Evaluated Models to Evaluation Aids: A Multi-Evidence Study of LLM-Based Difficulty Calibration for Programming Examinations. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.07523
title: Two forms of the AI difficulty ruler: solving-based and review-based evidence
description: The article distinguishes two forms of the AI ruler. The solving-based ruler has AI read problems, generate code, and submit to the online judge, producing process data such as pass rate, attempts, running time, and error type. The review-based ruler has AI provide structured scores for concept, implementation, debugging, complexity-risk, reading, and overall difficulty without submitting code. The article states the solving-based evidence "constitutes the empirical basis for choosing a unified reviewer in the subsequent review-based extension," while the review-based form is low-cost and scalable but lacks real judging feedback.
requirements: The review-based ruler must preserve reviewable source metadata such as model version, prompt hash, run date, endpoint, and sampling parameters, and its scores need validation against student performance, teacher judgment, or multi-reviewer agreement.
constraints: The review-based result "can only be interpreted as a preliminary/exploratory ruler and cannot replace a multi-reviewer consistency test," and the single-reviewer batch runs through a third-party endpoint whose model label cannot certify an official upstream model.
target_learning_goals: valid interpretation of programming-exam difficulty for item setting and parallel-class fairness
examples: Ten models solved an 8-problem exam synchronously with 120 students; a single reviewer scored 79, 26, and 106 problems via auditable API batches with archived prompts, schemas, and raw responses.

article_title: Uncovering adoption personas for generative AI in higher education: a clustering-based segmentation approach
citation: Afef Saihi and Vian Ahmed. (2026). Uncovering adoption personas for generative AI in higher education: a clustering-based segmentation approach. International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s41239-026-00583-z
title: Two-stage clustering pattern: hierarchical clustering to determine k, then k-means for final segmentation
description: A reusable analytical pattern for constructing user personas from survey data. In the first stage, "hierarchical agglomerative clustering, using Ward's linkage method and Euclidean distance" is applied, with dendrograms and silhouette coefficients informing the choice of cluster count. In the second stage, that optimal k is used as input for k-means clustering, a centroid-based algorithm valued for scalability and interpretability. Cluster quality is then assessed with internal validation indices such as the Silhouette Score, Calinski-Harabasz Index, and Davies-Bouldin Index.
requirements: Requires standardized composite variables and internal validation indices to justify the chosen number of clusters
constraints: The article notes the highest silhouette score occurred at k = 2, so the selected solution balanced statistical fit against interpretability rather than maximizing a single index
target_learning_goals: identifying latent user segments to inform educational technology design and support
examples: The study executed the clustering in Python's scikit-learn library and validated the four-cluster solution with Silhouette, Calinski-Harabasz, and Davies-Bouldin indices.

article_title: Special-R1: Reinforcement Learning for Special Education — Aligning LLM Tutors to Diverse Learners through Disability-Adaptive Training
citation: Unggi Lee, Jihoi Na, Yeil Jeong, Haeun Park, Yeonju Jang. (2026). Reinforcement Learning for Special Education: Aligning LLM Tutors to Diverse Learners through Disability-Adaptive Training. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.30670
title: Calibrate both the amount and the style of tutor support to the learner: support level from baseline accuracy, style from disability-specific access needs
description: The article argues effective special-education tutoring demands two simultaneous adjustments: the amount of support, calibrated to the learner's zone of proximal development, and the style of support, calibrated to disability-specific access needs through Explicit Instruction, the Prompting Hierarchy, High-Leverage Practices, and Universal Design for Learning. Special-R1 operationalizes both axes inside the tutor's system prompt and the judge of its thinking trace, and its ablations show the prompt-style axis is the single largest driver of persona-aware Fit gains. The framework treats these as orthogonal dimensions rather than a single generic pedagogical prompt.
requirements: A pre-measured baseline accuracy per problem type to select the support level, and a structured disability profile specifying recommended tutor strategies, communication patterns, and learning characteristics.
constraints: The Thinking Reward component of the framework only becomes effective when combined with adaptive prompting; under static prompts the accept/reject judge saturates.
target_learners: Learners with disabilities in one-on-one LLM tutoring
target_learning_goals: Scaffolded problem-solving support tailored to disability-specific access needs
examples: The tutor prompt variants SPED-static and SPED-adaptive draw style verbatim from the disability profile's tutor_strategies, communication_patterns, and learning_characteristics fields, with SPED-adaptive selecting the support level dynamically from baseline accuracy.

article_title: Flawed but Memorable: Student Critical Reception of Interest-Personalized GenAI Analogies in Computing Education
citation: Seth Bernstein and Naaz Sibia. 2026. Flawed but Memorable: Student Critical Reception of Interest-Personalized GenAI Analogies in Computing Education. Koli Calling '26. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.06095
title: Two-sided analogy auditing: target-domain and source-domain knowledge jointly support evaluation of an analogical mapping
description: The article's conceptual account of how learners evaluate analogies. Target-concept knowledge identifies the relations an analogy must preserve, while source-domain knowledge determines whether those relations hold there; the article states "neither side is sufficient alone." A familiar source may make an analogy both more engaging and more inspectable, giving interest personalization a possible epistemic role in addition to its motivational role. The account reframes expertise as source-domain or target-domain expertise rather than a single construct.
requirements: Evaluating an analogy requires knowledge of both the computing concept and the analogy's source domain
constraints: Because explanation format and personalization varied together in the design, the study cannot isolate personalization as the cause of the observed scrutiny
target_learners: undergraduate computing students who have completed CS2
target_learning_goals: critically evaluating AI-generated analogical explanations of computing concepts such as linked lists and recursion
examples: Participants who knew an analogy's source domain well, such as P6 with One Piece, audited the source side of the mapping directly and located the point of structural divergence.

article_title: Mapping the Distribution and Depth of Metacognitive Processes in Generative AI-Assisted Learning: Evidence from Interaction Logs and Concurrent Think-Aloud Protocols
citation: Li Shijin & Liu Junjian. (2026). Mapping the Distribution and Depth of Metacognitive Processes in Generative AI-Assisted Learning: Evidence from Interaction Logs and Concurrent Think-Aloud Protocols. Behavioral Sciences. https://doi.org/10.3390/bs16081365
title: Two-dimensional rubric coding operational process category and depth of explicit metacognitive evidence
description: The article introduces a shared coding rubric applied identically to interaction logs and think-aloud speech. "Dimension 1, operational process category, answered what metacognitive function was observable and assigned planning, monitoring, or regulation. Dimension 2, depth of explicit metacognitive evidence, answered how explicitly and integratively the unit articulated a goal, criterion, procedure, evaluation, or transfer and assigned implicit, awareness, strategic, or reflective." Depth is an ordinal property of the evidence in a semantic unit, not a taxonomy of processes or a measure of learner proficiency, and boundary rules govern ambiguous cases such as criterion-free versus criterion-tied judgments.
requirements: Trained double coding with consensus resolution; the reported agreement was process category κ = 0.90 (logs) and 0.87 (think-aloud), evidence depth κ = 0.86 and 0.85
constraints: The rubric classifies evidence in units rather than learners; its construct validity as a general scale has not been established, and separate unitization reliability was not reported
target_learners: undergraduate students in teacher-education and related majors
target_learning_goals: describing observable planning, monitoring, and regulation evidence in GenAI-assisted work
examples: A monitoring unit stating a concern without a criterion was coded awareness depth, while one invoking an observable-performance criterion was coded strategic depth

article_title: Applying the science of learning: Evidence-based principles for the design of multimedia instruction.
citation: Richard E. Mayer. (2008). Applying the Science of Learning: Evidence-Based Principles for the Design of Multimedia Instruction. American Psychologist. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0012841
title: Two-way street approach: reciprocal relation between science of learning and science of instruction
description: The article proposes that learning theory and educational practice stand in a reciprocal relation, contrasting this with a one-way street approach (theory applied to lessons) and a dead end street approach (theory divorced from authentic challenges). The article states that "in the two-way street approach, there is a reciprocal relation between learning theory and educational practice in which the science of learning must be expanded to be able to explain how learning works in authentic learning situations." It frames this as basic research on applied problems, inspired by Stokes's use-inspired basic research, and illustrates it with the 10 multimedia principles.
requirements: Research must address authentic learning situations while still testing learning theory
constraints: The article notes the one-way street approach yields theories of limited applicability beyond contrived lab settings
target_learning_goals: understanding how to design instruction that fosters learning
examples: The article's 10 multimedia principles are offered as an exemplar of merging theoretical and practical goals

description: The article's empirical apparatus consists of two experiments with Dutch-speaking EFL learners who viewed TV material, with vocabulary learning assessed through three measures. The design pairs viewing of audio-visual input with distinct receptive vocabulary knowledge measures, allowing learning to be detected at different levels of word knowledge.

article_title: Early Adverse Experiences and the Developing Brain
citation: Bick, J., Nelson, C. (2016). Early Adverse Experiences and the Developing Brain. Neuropsychopharmacol. https://doi.org/10.1038/npp.2015.252
title: Two distinct forms of early adversity: childhood maltreatment in family environments and extreme psychosocial deprivation in institutional rearing
description: The review organizes its account of early adversity around two distinct forms. The first is exposure to "childhood maltreatment in family environments", and the second is exposure to "extreme psychosocial deprivation in contexts of institutional rearing". The article treats these as separate experiences of adverse rearing, each imposing distinct challenges to the developing brain, and reviews evidence on each form's neurodevelopmental consequences and on intervention for each.
requirements: The framework applies to children exposed to these two adverse rearing conditions early in life.
constraints: The review's scope is limited to these two forms of adversity rather than all adverse experiences.

examples: The review devotes parallel treatment to maltreatment in family settings and to institutional rearing as its two focal adversity types.

article_title: Investigating Epistemic Stances in Game Play with Data Mining
citation: Martinez-Garza, M. M., & Clark, D. B. (2017). Investigating Epistemic Stances in Game Play with Data Mining. International Journal of Gaming and Computer-Mediated Simulations, 9(3). https://doi.org/10.4018/IJGCMS.2017070101
title: Two-System Framework (2SM) of game-based learning: player and learner stances organized around fast and slow cognition
description: The 2SM is a cognitive framework applying the two-system model of cognition to educational gaming. It holds that students build a second-order model of a game's encased simulation rather than an accurate mental analogue, and that play alternates between a fast, heuristic-driven player stance (System 1) and a slow, inquiry-oriented learner stance (System 2). The article states: "The premise of the 2SM framework is that students of educational games do not necessarily form accurate mental analogues of the software models that drive the phenomena they experience in-game". Through play students gather conditions, heuristics, and a second-order mental model.
requirements: Play data must be interpretable in terms of fast and slow processing strategies for the framework's stances to be operationalized
constraints: The framework was proposed as part of a general-use explanatory framework and its basic claims were still under investigation in this study
target_learning_goals: conceptual understanding of Newtonian kinematics
epistemic stances during game play
examples: In The Fuzzy Chronicles, the learner stance was operationalized as a Solve-and-Debug planning mode and the player stance as an Additive-Iterative mode

citation: Patricia A. Young. (2009). Instructional Design Frameworks and Intercultural Models. Information Science Reference, IGI Global. http://www.igi-global.com/reference
title: Twenty-five elements of culture as design factors, treated from anthropological, psychological, and scientific perspectives
description: CBM's Elements component is a taxonomy of culture for design, explicated "from an anthropological point of view, a psychological point of view, and a scientific point of view." The foreword states that "Twenty-five elements of culture are described and explained with examples from throughout the world," and notes these "are not elements that designers typically address." Examples include conceptions of what is beautiful, class and status, non-verbal communication traditions, behavior norms, emotional patterns, orientations toward time, and conceptions of intimate, personal, social and public space. Each element carries guiding questions for gathering culture data.
requirements: Designers use the range of questions provided to gather data related to each culture element
constraints: The taxonomy is selective: designers are advised to attend only to elements pertinent to a given project

citation: Haist Frank, Wazny Jarnet H., Toomarian Elizabeth, Adamo Maha. (2015). Development of brain systems for nonsymbolic numerosity and the relationship to formal math academic achievement. Human brain mapping. https://doi.org/10.1002/hbm.22666
title: Two-brain-systems developmental account of nonsymbolic numerosity contributions to math achievement
description: The article proposes that "two different brain systems for nonsymbolic numerosity acuity may contribute to individual differences in math achievement and that the contribution of these systems differs across development." One system is the lateral parietal/IPS approximate number system, whose achievement link is restricted to children; the other is a ventral occipital-temporal visual discrimination system, active in children and adults with shifting regional foci. The account explains why behavioral measures fail while neural measures detect achievement relationships.

standardized math achievement and IQ measures to control for general cognitive ability
constraints: the parietal achievement link is restricted to children in this sample
the sample comprised typical through high-achieving individuals, so extension to low-achieving samples is untested

citation: Kim, Y.-S., Al Otaiba, S., Sidler Folsom, J., & Gruelich, L. (2013). Language, literacy, attentional behaviors, and instructional quality predictors of written composition for first graders. Early Childhood Research Quarterly, 28(3), 461–469. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ecresq.2013.01.001

description: The article adopts a trait-based evaluation of written composition in which seven rated aspects (ideas, organization, word choice, sentence flow, spelling, mechanics, handwriting) load onto 'two related (r = .65) but dissociable latent variables': a substantive quality dimension (ideas, organization, word choice, sentence flow) and a writing conventions dimension (spelling, mechanics, handwriting). This structure, established via confirmatory factor analysis in prior work by the authors, served as the outcome framework for the study's multilevel models.

constraints: The voice aspect was excluded due to a floor effect for first-grade children in preliminary work

title: Two-factor model of executive function in kindergarten: inhibition and WM–flexibility as separate dimensions
description: A latent-variable account of executive function in kindergarten children in which "inhibition and working memory (WM)–flexibility were separate dimensions." The model was derived from confirmatory factor analysis of six EF measures and served as the structural basis for predicting later math achievement. It treats EF in this age group as two distinguishable components rather than a unitary capacity.

constraints: Structure established for kindergarten-age children in this sample

article_title: The longitudinal relationship between early inhibitory control skills and emergent literacy in preschool children
citation: Gandolfi, E., Traverso, L., Zanobini, M., Usai, M. C., & Viterbori, P. (2021). The longitudinal relationship between early inhibitory control skills and emergent literacy in preschool children. Reading and Writing. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11145-021-10131-y
title: Two-component organization of inhibitory control in early childhood: response inhibition and interference suppression
description: The article adopts a conceptualization of inhibitory control as "a set of sub-functions rather than a unique individual ability, already in early preschool years", distinguishing two components that emerge by approximately three years of age. Response inhibition is "the ability to suppress a dominant but inappropriate response in order to display a weaker but more adequate one", assessed with the Circle Drawing task. Interference suppression "develops later than response inhibition and involves the ability to suppress interfering information and to select the piece of information one has to respond to", assessed with the Fish flanker task. The study uses this distinction to test which component longitudinally supports emergent literacy.
requirements: Tasks must tap the two components distinctly; the authors chose two tasks "to maximize the difference between response inhibition and interference suppression processes, taking the suitability of the task for toddlers into account".
constraints: The authors note "this type of organization is not universally accepted (Joyce et al., 2016)" and that research on the latent organization of inhibitory control in childhood has provided mixed results.
target_learners: typically developing monolingual toddlers aged 28–36 months
target_learning_goals: emergent literacy precursors: phonological awareness and early orthographic knowledge
examples: Children moved puppets along a circle as slowly as possible (Circle Drawing) and pointed to the direction of a central target fish flanked by interfering fishes (Fish task) in a 20-min day-care session.

article_title: Non-symbolic arithmetic abilities and mathematics achievement in the first year of formal schooling
citation: Gilmore Camilla K., McCarthy Shannon E., Spelke Elizabeth S. (2010). Non-symbolic arithmetic abilities and achievement in the first year of formal schooling in mathematics. Cognition. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cognition.2010.02.002
title: Two-source account of symbolic mathematics mastery: prior non-symbolic numerical abilities plus acquired symbol mastery
description: The article proposes that mastery of symbolic mathematics has two sources: non-symbolic numerical abilities that are present prior to schooling in arithmetic and exist across a broad economic spectrum, and symbol mastery that is acquired during childhood and is accelerated for advantaged children. The account explains why non-symbolic abilities predict school mathematics while socioeconomic gaps persist in achievement but not in non-symbolic tasks. It rests on the finding that "children in the wealthier community outperformed the less advantaged children on the symbolic arithmetic task" in prior work, while non-symbolic abilities were similar across communities.

Acquisition of number words and Arabic symbols during childhood
constraints: The article states there is mixed evidence concerning the relationship between non-symbolic numerical abilities and number word mastery, and further research with younger children is needed to distinguish causal directions

target_learning_goals: Early symbolic number and arithmetic learning

citation: van de Kamp, M.-T., Admiraal, W., & Rijlaarsdam, G. (2016). Becoming original: effects of strategy instruction. Instructional Science, 44, 543–566. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-016-9384-y

description: The article presents a matrix of twelve divergent thinking activities organised along two dimensions: remoteness (the metaphorical distance from a stimulus, running from free association to bisociation) and abstractness (running from association through combination to abstraction). The authors state they "built a model of twelve divergent thinking activities, along two dimensions—remoteness and abstractness" to serve as a framework for teaching students how to generate more original ideas deliberately in visual arts education. article_title: The effect of short online pedagogical training on university teachers’ interpretations of teaching–learning situations
citation: Henna Vilppu, Ilona Södervik, Liisa Postareff, Mari Murtonen. (2019). The effect of short online pedagogical training on university teachers’ interpretations of teaching–learning situations. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-019-09496-z
title: Two-phase online module design combining individual reflective essays with small-group peer discussion
description: Each short online pedagogy module comprised “an individual study phase and a small-group phase”. In the individual phase, participants studied self-study materials (videos, articles, glossaries, quizzes) and wrote a reflective essay; in the small-group phase, groups of four to six shared and commented on each other’s essays in Google Docs, with experienced teachers and novices mixed in each group. The design aims to support co-construction of knowledge and conceptual change regarding educational concepts, and all tasks were designed so that doctoral students without teaching experience could complete them.

A teacher role that monitors discussion and gives personal written feedback after each module
target_learners: Doctoral students, including those without teaching duties
target_learning_goals: Conceptual development and change about teaching
Shared understanding of pedagogical concepts
examples: The three modules used were Becoming a Teacher, How to Plan My Teaching, and Lecturing and Expertise; each included essay writing followed by peer commenting.

article_title: Investigating construct validity of cognitive load measurement using single-item subjective rating scales
citation: Schuessler, K., Fischer, V., & Walpuski, M. (2025). Investigating construct validity of cognitive load measurement using single-item subjective rating scales. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-024-09692-6
title: Cognitive load as an at least two-dimensional construct with a task-difficulty component and an invested-effort component
description: Following Paas (1992), the article treats cognitive load as "an at least two-dimensional concept". One component, perceived task or item difficulty, "refers to the requirements of the task" and task-learner interactions (Paas's mental load); the other, invested mental effort, "refers to the cognitive capacity a learner invests to accomplish task demands". This definition concerns overall load and deliberately does not separate intrinsic from extraneous load. The study operationalizes the two components with the two dominant single-item rating scales and models them as two Rasch dimensions.
requirements: Measurement must distinguish which component is being rated, because the task-difficulty item pertains mainly to the task while the effort item pertains to a process involving more aspects than only the task.
constraints: The definition refers to overall load and does not differentiate between intrinsic and extraneous cognitive load.
target_learners: learners working on chemistry competence tasks
target_learning_goals: understanding and measuring overall cognitive load during learning and performance
examples: The study measured both components after each task with single-item 7-point rating scales adapted from Paas (1992) and Marcus et al. (1996), then estimated them as two separate Rasch dimensions.

article_title: Bridging domains: examining the effects of relevance instructions and guiding questions on pre-service teachers’ first- and second-order knowledge integration
citation: Lehmann, T. (2024). Bridging domains: examining the effects of relevance instructions and guiding questions on pre-service teachers' first- and second-order knowledge integration. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-023-09655-3
title: Two-layer conceptualization of pre-service teachers' knowledge integration: first-order and second-order KI
description: The article adopts Lehmann's (2020b) conceptualization in which knowledge integration has two layers. First-order KI denotes "the cognitive-constructive learning processes of building and structuring an integrated knowledge base within one's memory", while second-order KI "denotes the integrated use of domain-specific knowledge" in application situations such as teaching, lesson planning, and task design. The framework connects to models of teachers' professional competence (disposition vs. situation-specific performance) and to transfer theory, and it underpins the study's mediation hypothesis.
requirements: Learning settings must involve multiple domain-specific knowledge bodies (e.g., CK, PK, PCK) that can be interrelated
constraints: The article notes empirical studies on the relation between integration in learning and in application settings are scarce and findings vary
target_learning_goals: integration of content knowledge, general pedagogical knowledge, and pedagogical-content knowledge
integrated application of professional knowledge in teaching tasks
examples: The study operationalized first-order KI via essay coding (elaborations across domains, switches) and second-order KI via an integrated knowledge application test on a lesson plan

article_title: Metacognitive awareness in relation to university students’ learning profiles
citation: Tuononen, T., Hyytinen, H., Räisänen, M., Hailikari, T., & Parpala, A. (2023). Metacognitive awareness in relation to university students' learning profiles. Metacognition and Learning, 18, 37–54. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-022-09314-x
title: Two-component model of metacognitive awareness: knowledge about cognition and regulation of cognition
description: The article defines metacognitive awareness as "students' awareness of their own learning strategies and also of how, when and why to successfully apply them" and says it comprises two dimensions: knowledge about cognition and regulation of cognition. Knowledge about cognition covers declarative, procedural and conditional knowledge of cognition; regulation of cognition is the ability to plan, implement, monitor and evaluate learning processes across three cyclical, intertwined phases. The study's factor analyses tested and supported this two-component structure in a multidisciplinary higher education sample.
requirements: Assessment relies on self-report instruments (the shortened MAI) that ask students to reflect on their own strategies and regulation
constraints: The CFA fit indexes were only acceptable-to-modest, and the article states further development of the MAI in the multidisciplinary higher education context would be important
target_learners: Third-year bachelor's students in humanities, social sciences and theology
target_learning_goals: Metacognitive awareness of one's own learning processes
Regulation of studying

article_title: Reactivity to confidence ratings in older individuals performing the latin square task
citation: Double, K. S., & Birney, D. P. (2018). Reactivity to confidence ratings in older individuals performing the latin square task. Metacognition and Learning, 13, 309–326. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-018-9186-5
title: Two-stage model of reactivity to confidence ratings
description: The article proposes a two-stage account of why eliciting confidence ratings changes performance. In the first stage, performing CR makes participants attend to confidence-related beliefs, i.e. they "rely on information-based cues"; in the second stage, participants make strategic control decisions such as speed-accuracy trade-offs based on those activated beliefs, which then affect task performance. The model explains why high-confidence participants persist longer and low-confidence participants disengage, and why CR can reinforce existing beliefs whether or not they are accurate.
requirements: Confidence ratings must direct attention to information participants would not otherwise attend to for reactivity to occur
constraints: Proposed from a single experiment with older adults; the authors state substantially more work is needed to establish robustness and generalisability
target_learners: older adult community samples performing timed problem-solving tasks
target_learning_goals: metacognitive monitoring and control during reasoning and problem solving
examples: In the experiment, high-confidence CR participants persisted longer per item while low-confidence CR participants answered more quickly, consistent with belief-driven control decisions

article_title: How accurate and predictive are judgments of solvability? Explorations in a two-phase anagram solving paradigm
citation: Burton, O. R., Bodner, G. E., Williamson, P., & Arnold, M. M. (2023). How accurate and predictive are judgments of solvability? Explorations in a two-phase anagram solving paradigm. Metacognition and Learning, 18, 1–35. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-022-09313-y
title: Two-phase JOS paradigm separating intuitive solvability judgments from later solving outcomes
description: The two-phase paradigm separates the JOS phase, where participants make intuitive solvability judgments for an entire set of problems, from a subsequent solving phase where solving outcomes and effort regulation are measured. This design avoids the confound of interleaved paradigms, in which "JOSs may be influenced by solving attempts, and vice versa", allowing reasoners to bootstrap their JOS intuitions. The article uses this paradigm across three experiments with anagram durations parametrically manipulated across blocks.
requirements: JOS phase must precede the solving phase so judgments capture intuitions before reasoning occurs
Participants must be able to report already-solved (AS) judgments so spontaneously solved items can be excluded from discrimination and predictiveness measures
constraints: Interleaved paradigms may inflate JOS discrimination and predictiveness relative to the two-phase approach
Spontaneous solving during the JOS phase confounds measurement if not separately reported
target_learning_goals: accurate meta-reasoning monitoring of problem solvability
effective effort regulation during problem solving
examples: In Experiment 3 the solving phase included both solvable and unsolvable anagrams with self-regulated solving time, enabling measurement of not-solvable responses as an effort-regulation measure
key_sources: Burton, O. R., Bodner, G. E., Williamson, P., & Arnold, M. M. (2023). How accurate and predictive are judgments of solvability? Explorations in a two-phase anagram solving paradigm. Metacognition and Learning, 18, 1–35. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-022-09313-y

article_title: Metacognition, achievement goals, study strategies and academic achievement: pathways to achievement
citation: Anneke Vrugt & Frans J. Oort. (2008). Metacognition, achievement goals, study strategies and academic achievement: pathways to achievement. Metacognition Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-008-9022-4
title: Two-pathway model of effective self-regulated learning: a metacognitive pathway and a strategy pathway
description: The article proposes and tests a causal model in which achievement goals (mastery, performance-approach, performance-avoidance), metacognition (knowledge, regulation, experience), and four study strategy types jointly determine exam scores. As the abstract states, "effective self-regulated learning involved two pathways: a metacognitive and a strategy pathway." The metacognitive pathway runs from mastery goals through metacognition to all four strategies; the strategy pathway carries direct effects of mastery and performance-approach goals on strategies, bypassing metacognition. The model was tested with structural equation modeling controlling for intellectual ability, gender and age.
requirements: Requires measures of achievement goals, metacognition, study strategies and achievement, plus control of intellectual ability, gender and age as the article did
constraints: The fitted model required adding direct goal-to-strategy paths beyond the hypothesized indirect structure; the negative avoidance-to-metacognition path held only for effective self-regulators
target_learning_goals: academic achievement in an introductory course
self-regulated learning skills
examples: The model was fitted separately to 421 effective and 383 less effective self-regulators distinguished by effort expenditure on MSLQ effort regulation items

article_title: Sequential and temporal characteristics of self and socially regulated learning
citation: Inge Molenaar & Sanna Järvelä. (2014). Sequential and temporal characteristics of self and socially regulated learning. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-014-9114-2
title: Two views on temporality in S-SRL research: events in a continuous flow versus relative arrangements among multiple events
description: The editorial proposes that existing research on the temporal characteristics of S-SRL can be viewed through two distinct perspectives. The first "views events in a continuous flow", analyzing the positioning, duration and rate of individual S-SRL actions during learning. The second "analyzes relative arrangement among multiple events", focusing on the organization of actions over time, including development of sequential characteristics and transformations of sequences. The special-issue studies combine these perspectives to differing degrees.
requirements: Online measurement of S-SRL as a series of events, since all contributors used online measurement and view the construct as a series of events
constraints: The special issue constitutes only a first step towards understanding the sequential and temporal characteristics of S-SRL
target_learning_goals: understanding and supporting self and socially regulated learning processes
examples: Kuvalja et al. and Malmberg et al. incorporated both perspectives, showing they provide different insights into sequential and temporal characteristics of self-regulatory behaviour and strategy use

article_title: Signaling task awareness in think-aloud protocols from students selecting relevant information from text
citation: Gonny L. M. Schellings & Hein Broekkamp. (2011). Signaling task awareness in think-aloud protocols from students selecting relevant information from text. Metacognition and Learning 6:65–82. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-010-9067-z
title: Two-level model of task awareness in text selection (global and local task levels)
description: The article conceives task awareness as conscious task representation operating at two levels. As printed: "Task awareness runs at two levels. At the global level, selection goals and the task's instructions are represented, while at the local level, reflections about specific text parts are involved." Global representations concern major task components, selection goals, text or task difficulty, and time available; local representations are bound to specific text units such as particular words or concepts. The study operationalised these levels in a coding instrument applied to think-aloud protocols of text selection.
requirements: Task awareness can only be observed when learners verbalize about it, since it is defined as a conscious representation of the selection process
constraints: Think-aloud data capture only higher-order, non-automatized activities that consume working-memory room, per the Ericsson and Simon framework the article cites
target_learning_goals: awareness of task demands when selecting relevant information from instructional texts
examples: Twelve tenth-graders thought aloud while performing linguistic, educational, and personal selection tasks on three biology texts; verbalizations were coded into global- and local-level categories

article_title: Reading behavior as an indicator of comprehension monitoring when reading expository texts
citation: Catharina Tibken, Simon P. Tiffin-Richards. (2025). Reading behavior as an indicator of comprehension monitoring when reading expository texts. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-025-09440-2
title: Two-Step Model of Validation: passive validation detects inconsistencies, but resolving them requires metacognitive effort
description: The Two-Step Model of Validation (Richter & Maier, 2017) assumes readers "can detect inconsistent information through non-strategic, passive validation processes, but fully processing and potentially resolving inconsistencies requires metacognitive resources and effort (strategic elaboration)". The article uses this model, alongside the Content-Source Integration Model, to motivate its hypotheses: first-pass disruptions reflect passive validation, whereas reanalysis reflects strategic, reader-initiated metacognitive regulation. The study's finding that reanalysis, not first-pass reading, predicted inconsistency identification is consistent with this account.
requirements: Readers must perceive the text as demanding or hold high standards of coherence for metacognitive effort to be engaged
constraints: The article applies the model to (short) expository texts about conceptually difficult topics read for study purposes
target_learners: university students and other experienced adult readers learning from expository texts
target_learning_goals: metacognitive comprehension monitoring and regulation during reading
construction of a coherent situation model of expository text content
examples: The study measured first-pass reading time and lookbacks as indicators of passive validation, and rereading time and revisits as indicators of strategic reanalysis, across target word, sentence-final word, and pre-target text areas

citation: Rosário, Pedro José Sales Luís de Fonseca; Núñez Pérez, José Carlos; Ferrando, Pere J.; Paiva, Olimpia; Lourenço, Abilio; Cerezo Menéndez, Rebeca; Valle Arias, Antonio. (2013). title: Two-level structural equation model for approaches to teaching and studying in biology
description: The article's organizing analytic framework is a "two-level structural equation model", as stated in its title, applied to the study of "biology achievement in high school". The two-level structure indicates the model represents variables simultaneously at two hierarchical levels of schooling data, and the framework ties teachers' approaches to teaching to students' approaches to studying and achievement. Because only the metadata record is supplied, the model's indicators, levels and estimation details cannot be described beyond what the title and citation lines print.

approaches to studying
examples: The article's own design, announced in its title: a two-level structural equation model relating approaches to teaching and approaches to studying to biology achievement in high school

article_title: Enhancing the Peer-Feedback Process Through Instructional Support: A Meta-Analysis
citation: Hornstein, J., Keller, M. V., Greisel, M., Dresel, M., & Kollar, I. (2025). Enhancing the Peer-Feedback Process Through Instructional Support: A Meta-Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10017-3
title: Two-dimensional framework for classifying instructional support in peer-feedback: phase (provision vs. reception) and specificity (content-specific vs. generic)
description: The article proposes two orthogonal ways to differentiate instructional support in peer-feedback scenarios. The first distinguishes support by the phase in which it is presented — feedback provision vs. feedback reception — within the five-phase peer-feedback process (design, task performance, provision, reception, evaluation). The second distinguishes support by specificity: content-specific support focuses on "the application of specific knowledge in a selected subject area", whereas generic support assists students independently of content, e.g. prompting feed up, feed back, and feed forward. The meta-analysis applies both categorizations to estimate differential effects.
requirements: Peer-feedback scenarios in which a control condition receives peer-feedback without the instructional support being evaluated, so effects can be attributed to the support alone
constraints: The two categorizations are orthogonal: the same presentation mode (rubrics, questions, sentence starters) can be either content-specific or generic
target_learning_goals: Providing high-quality peer-feedback
Processing and using received peer-feedback
Acquiring subject-matter-related knowledge
examples: The meta-analysis coded each included study's support by phase and by specificity, then pooled effects separately for each cell, e.g. generic support during feedback provision on subject-matter-related knowledge.

article_title: Perfectionism in Academically Gifted Students: A Systematic Review
citation: Grugan, M. C., Hill, A. P., Madigan, D. J., Donachie, T. C., Olsson, L. F., & Etherson, M. E. (2021). Perfectionism and Academically Gifted Students: A Systematic Review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-021-09597-7
title: Two-factor higher-order model of perfectionism (PS vs PC) as the review's organising framework
description: The review organises all evidence using the two-factor higher-order model of perfectionism (Stoeber & Otto, 2006), which integrates different perfectionism measures into two dimensions. Perfectionistic strivings subsume "aspects of perfectionism associated with self-oriented striving for perfection and the setting of very high personal performance standards". Perfectionistic concerns subsume concerns about mistakes, fear of negative evaluation, and negative reactions to imperfection. The review classifies subscales from F-MPS, HF-MPS, CAPS, APS-R and PNPS as PS or PC indicators.
requirements: Studies must use multidimensional perfectionism measures whose subscales can be classified as PS or PC indicators
constraints: Some indicators such as organisation and order subscales are peripheral facets that may load on a third factor independent of PS and PC
target_learners: young students identified as academically gifted
target_learning_goals: understanding personality correlates of academic achievement and well-being in gifted learners
examples: The review categorised the personal standards subscale of the F-MPS and socially prescribed perfectionism subscales of the HF-MPS and CAPS as PS and PC indicators respectively

article_title: A Systematic Mapping Literature Review on Two-Eyed Seeing in P-20 Education
citation: Gardner-Vandy, K., Utley, J., Just, A., Hathcock, S., & Stansberry, S. (2025). A Systematic Mapping Literature Review on Two-Eyed Seeing in P-20 Education. Review of Educational Research. https://doi.org/10.3102/00346543251329570
title: Two-Eyed Seeing (Etuaptmumk) as a pedagogical approach interweaving Indigenous and Western ways of knowing
description: Two-Eyed Seeing (TES), in Mi'kmaq Etuaptmumk, was originally presented by Mi'kmaq Elder Albert Marshall in 2004. It "refers to learning to see from one eye with the strengths of Indigenous ways of knowing and from the other eye with the strengths of western ways of knowing and to using both of these eyes together" (Hatcher et al., 2009a, p. 146). A TES approach weaves Indigenous and Western knowledges, implies "responsibilities for reciprocity, mutual accountability, and co-learning" (Hogue & Bartlett, 2014), seeks commonalities between the two sciences while respecting differences, and aims to eliminate conflicts between them. Elder Marshall described TES as "a guiding principle that covers all aspects of our lives," applicable beyond science education.
requirements: Requires interweaving rather than side-by-side introduction of the two knowledge systems, with Indigenous knowledge holders included as part of the process
constraints: The review limits its scope to TES specifically, excluding other frameworks that merge Indigenous knowledges with Western science
target_learners: P-20 students, including Indigenous students in formal educational settings
target_learning_goals: Interweaving Indigenous ways of knowing with Western science to increase Indigenous students' engagement with content
examples: TES was first used at Cape Breton University in Nova Scotia in an integrative science program devised to encourage Mi'kmaw students to pursue science and science-related programs
